overview: Pequot communities belong to southeastern Connecticut along Long Island Sound. Their seventeenth-century influence grew through coastal resources and exchange. Mashantucket Pequot and Eastern Pequot peoples continue this history as distinct communities. The imported coastal outline and its 1492 to 1500 interval are limited map coverage, not the boundaries of either modern reservation or dates for the existence of the people.

periods.title: Homeland and regional influence
periods.summary: Pequot communities participated in coastal exchange before colonial conflict escalated.

periods.title: War and imposed dispersal
periods.summary: The Pequot War and Hartford treaty brought killings, captivity and attempted political erasure.

periods.title: Continuing Pequot communities
periods.summary: Survivors rebuilt community in Connecticut despite repeated dispossession.

items.text: Early seventeenth-century Pequot communities produced and traded wampum and dealt with Dutch and English newcomers. Access to Long Island Sound supported their regional economic power. Increasing colonial competition and demands developed alongside epidemics and tensions among neighboring nations.

On May 26, 1637, English forces and Native allies attacked the fortified Pequot settlement at Mistick. Fire and killing destroyed the village and took many civilian lives. The battlefield project reconstructs the campaign from documents and archaeology, while acknowledging that the conflict extended beyond this single attack.

The 1638 Treaty of Hartford was negotiated by English, Mohegan and Narragansett leaders. It assigned surviving Pequots to other communities and sought to prohibit their Pequot name and return to their homeland. A treaty could demand that a people disappear on paper; it could not make their kinship and identity vanish.

Pequot leader Robin Cassacinamon helped survivors return to Connecticut lands. His community settled at Morgan’s Point in Noank following permission in 1651, before moving to Mashantucket, where a reservation was established in 1666. This rebuilding followed the war rather than beginning an unrelated population.

Eastern Pequot families settled near Long Pond and Lantern Hill by the 1670s, with a formal reservation deed in 1683. The community’s continuing history includes farming, hunting, basket making and gatherings. This reservation history should not be confused with the separate Mashantucket community farther west.

The Pequot Museum’s eighteenth-century farmstead reconstruction explains root cellars identified at several reservation farmsteads. Stone foundations covered with logs and earth kept stored food cool in summer. Before an electric refrigerator, the ground itself could help protect the household’s food supply.

The same guide places herb gardens close to eighteenth-century houses for cooking and medicinal use. It also explains refuse pits, where discarded objects now help archaeologists investigate past households. A rubbish pile can be a wonderfully informative document, though its former owners probably did not plan it that way.

Children collected low-bush blueberries in baskets, according to the farmstead guide. Berries could be eaten fresh, dried for later use or crushed for dye. The guide separately identifies apple and peach orchards as developments after European introduction, keeping colonial-era foods distinct from earlier harvests.

Milkweed and dogbane provided fibers for cordage and woven work. The museum guide distinguishes silkier milkweed for finely twined bags and belts from dogbane’s more utilitarian uses. Choosing a plant meant considering what the finished object needed to do.

Since 2003, Eastern Pequot people and University of Massachusetts Boston archaeologists have worked together on reservation research. The nation reports recovering ten housing sites with pottery and other household objects. In 2019, the collection moved to the Mashantucket Pequot Museum at the Eastern Pequot council’s request, preserving Eastern Pequot ownership of the story.

The Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation publishes “Wuyeepuyôq,” translated as “Welcome,” on its website. This short attested sample is contemporary written Pequot used by a living government. It is not an invented fifteenth-century inscription or a claim that modern spelling remained unchanged through earlier centuries.

The museum’s current seasonal account links the Green Corn Moon with Schemitzun, a harvest celebration, and describes winter as a time for sharing stories and histories. These community explanations show how food, social gatherings and teaching remain connected in later Pequot life.

Congress’s 1983 settlement act recognized the Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation and funded land repurchase. Its later economic experiments included a lettuce farm, a quarry and a pizza restaurant before a successful bingo operation opened in 1986. Rebuilding a government also required finding ways to support housing, work and health care.

The Eastern Pequot nation reports that Connecticut approved funding in 2021 for a community septic system, a well, road improvements and tribal-office infrastructure. This is a modern funding decision, not a completed-project claim. Water, sanitation and usable roads belong in a people’s history alongside diplomacy and warfare.

ending.text: Colonial warfare shattered Pequot political power and dispersed survivors, but Pequot communities continued. Mashantucket Pequot and Eastern Pequot histories carry that continuity in distinct institutions. The imported map ending at 1500 is not a historical extinction date.
